utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Firstly, the Chamber would like to deal with some decisions that remain to be delivered. There will be filed today and distributed the Chamber's decision in respect of the question of two expert witnesses which the Prosecution wish to call. We -- reasons are set out in that decision. The conclusion to which we have come is that the Chamber should hear the evidence of the two witnesses, but that they should be available for cross-examination. And we recognise that many of the matters raised by counsel for the Defence in their submission will be relevant to and have to be weighed by the Tribunal as a matter of weight in our evaluation of the evidence. With respect to the motion of the Defence requesting assistance in the matter of the recent interviews that were made available to them with the witness Miodrag Jokic, interviews conducted by the Prosecution this year which have been made available in disk and/or tape form, it was thought that we should order or require that these disks and tapes be produced in transcript form and that cross-examination of Admiral Jokic be further delayed until that could be done. There have been earlier submissions on more than one occasion with respect to this matter, and earlier decisions of the Chamber. I won't go over those matters again. They remain pertinent in respect of this decision. In our view, it is not a case which raises the principle of the equality of arms, as is submitted by the Defence. The Defence has had, for some time, notice of the essential evidence upon which the Prosecution would rely in respect of Admiral Jokic. The Defence has been provided very late, regrettably late, with this additional interview material with the Admiral, but the Defence has now had that material for a time enough to review and evaluate its content. It's not that they are deprived of this material; the pertinent issue is that they will not have the advantage of it in transcript form as well as in disk and tape form when it comes to cross-examination. In the Chamber's view, that does not preclude the adequate use of this material by the Defence in the cross-examination of the Admiral. It may make the process slower and less efficient. For that, there can be no fault put on the Defence. It is due entirely to the late making available of that information to them. But nevertheless, the cross-examination, so far as this material may raise any material new matter, apart from that which the Defence had already adequate notice, in our view, may be adequately dealt with in cross-examination, despite the inconvenience to which we've adverted. In our view, there's no question of any basic right to a fair trial being effected in this matter. So having regard to the fact that it would involve, we are told, at least some two weeks' work to translate, and there will be difficulty fitting in that work - I use the word "translate," I should have said "transcribe" - and that there will be difficulty fitting that work in for those responsible for performing the task, we think there will be less interruption and delay in the trial if the evidence now continues and cross-examination is conducted without the added assistance of a transcript. With respect to the Defence motion for cross-examination of medical witnesses as to the question of the fitness of the accused to stand trial, we would observe immediately that this is not an issue regulated by rule. It must be determined according to the particular circumstances affecting this issue, and the Chamber must be guided by fairness and the interests of justice. In that light, we find ourselves persuaded by some of the submissions of Mr. Petrovic, but we could more reliably evaluate the competing reports if we had the advantage of hearing cross-examination in which the opposing party can test the qualifications, experience, the approach, and the conclusions of the author or authors of the main expert report of the other side. In the Chamber's conclusion, therefore, there should be an opportunity for cross-examination. However, we make it clear that this opportunity will not be unrestricted. These are expert medical reports. There is no wide factual divergency, as with most of the ordinary witnesses in this case. The points of professional divergence and their merits can be adequately identified and explored in a limited time. Further, where more than one expert has joined in a report, it is not, in our view, necessary for every one of the authors to be called, to be available for cross-examination, as the relevant issues for present purposes can be identified and explored with any one of the authors. Therefore, in the Chamber's view, first, at least one of the expert authors of the primary Prosecution report should be called to give evidence. We would indicate that more than one may be called, should the Prosecution see reason for this, but in our view at least one should be called. Secondly, the expert author of the Defence report should be called to give evidence. Thirdly, expert authors may give evidence by videolink, if that is more practical. If this is desired in any particular case, any necessary formal procedural steps, including any further orders that may be necessary, should be dealt with and obtained by the party calling the particular witness. So we leave it to each party to make any administrative steps and obtain any further orders that prove necessary. Fourthly, when each expert author is called, we do not presently anticipate the need for other than short formal evidence-in-chief, essentially identifying and tendering the report or reports that have been produced by that party. As we have indicated, we accept the views advanced by the Defence. The main purpose of the hearing is to enable cross-examination, and that should be the area to which time is devoted. We will limit the time of cross-examination. Our intention is that we should be able to deal with this whole issue in one sitting day. That means that we would normally anticipate that cross-examination of a particular witness should not take longer than one hour. Given the nature of the issues which we have briefly indicated earlier, in that time it should be possible to identify areas of significant divergence and put opposing views and principles. Re-examination will, again, be limited. We cannot imagine that it would take longer than 10 or 15 minutes. Fifthly, the parties should liaise with each other and with the Chamber's senior legal officer, Ms. Musser, to coordinate a suitable date for the evidence of these witnesses. In this respect the Chamber would remind both parties for the need the Chamber strongly feels to conclude consideration of this critical issue. It's been outstanding for too long, in the Chamber's view. Sixthly, while we have confined our order to the two primary reports, one of the Prosecution and one of the Defence, leave is given for the Prosecution to formally prove the MRI scan, which was performed this year in The Hague, and the expert evaluation of it. And leave is also given to either party to call any other expert whose opinion has been taken into account of the expert author of the primary report of that party. We give that leave and open that possibility in case either party is concerned that there may be some subsidiary expert issue that ought at least to be more formally placed before the Tribunal. If there is such a need, and apart from the MRI scan we don't see it at the moment, but if there is such a need we would expect that the treatment of that issue will be brief indeed, and it too can be accommodated in the one sitting day along with the other matters. So we've granted those leaves, more out of caution and for convenience rather than out of a concern by the Chamber that there really is something there that must be dealt with. So please understand that neither party needs to think they must come along with somebody else; that's not the position. But if you see that there is a need for somebody whose work is identified but perhaps not sufficiently explained in what is before us, the opportunity is there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Now, that will be quite a bit for the parties to absorb and evaluate, but I think within what has been indicated by the Chamber is sufficient to indicate the course and the format which we propose with respect to the dealing with this important issue. We certainly think it ought to be possible to get the evidence over in one sitting day with the sort of discipline and restraints that we have indicated, but with considerable advantage to the Chamber, as Mr. Petrovic has submitted, in having the opportunity to hear the opposing view put to each witness and any potential or submitted deficiencies in the expert's approach, identified, and exposed, and tested. We hope that day when that evidence can be dealt with will occur in the near future, and we would certainly be prepared to interpose that day in the course of other evidence that is progressing, as soon as convenient times can be identified. I think we are now ready to proceed with the evidence of the witness, if the witness could be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Admiral. If I could remind you of the affirmation you took at the commencement of your evidence, it still applies. Now, I think you have matters to finalise, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in conclusion, I wanted to just cover a couple of matters upon review of the transcripts that I thought needed to be addressed, and then proceed with a video we discussed with the Chamber before we retired with Admiral Jokic the last time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, can you confirm that General Strugar, as the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, was commanding both land and naval forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has tendered into evidence through you during the previous days of your testimony several combat orders -- shall I start again? Are you hearing me okay, Admiral? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear you well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has tendered into evidence through you during the previous days of your testimony several combat orders issued by the 9th VPS. Can you confirm that all such combat orders issued by the 9th VPS were pursuant to orders of the 2nd Operational Group command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In connection with the shelling of the Old Town in October of 1991, in November of 1991, and in December, particularly December -- speaking of December 6th, 1991, do you know if the JNA or the JA, however you wish to refer to it, ever removed or brought formal criminal charges - again, to your knowledge - against General Strugar, Captain Vladimir Kovacevic, yourself, Milan Zec, Colonel Gavrilo Kovacevic, Major Komar or Colonel Gojko Djurasic. We'll go one by one. Were any charges in connection with the shelling incidents, charges or removal, brought, to your knowledge, against General Pavle Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Against yourself, Admiral Jokic, in connection with these incidents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Against Captain Vladimir Kovacevic, the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Trebinje -- of the 472nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Gavrilo Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Major Komar, the Chief of Staff of the Trebinje Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I also add Obrad Vicic, the commander of the Trebinje Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Gojko Djurasic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, did you retire with an honourable discharge? Excuse me, before I ask you this question. I've just given you a list of names of persons. Is there any other person that the JNA brought criminal charges against or removed as a result of the shellings that I have indicated against the Old Town of Dubrovnik? I've only given you a list. Is there any other person you can cite that was criminally charged and/or removed for these acts, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, did you retire honourably, with an honourable discharge?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say how I left, then you can assess it. In the decision on my retirement, it said that I retired at my own request, which was not true. I then said that I did not want to retire under those conditions. I did not ask to retire; they were retiring me prematurely, a few years prematurely. I did not have an order on appointment, appointment as commander of the sector. This order stayed back in Belgrade and I never received it. I also got a pension that was much lower than that that my assistants got. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you believe -- well, perhaps you can explain why you were prematurely retired. Would you explain what your belief is.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that there were some differences in terms of command. First of all, I did not mince my words. And from time to time I disagreed with the way in which the operation was being conducted. And before that, I was very critical vis-a-vis the regime, and the euphoria that prevailed then in society, in politics, and in the military. That was manifested earlier on when I was a cabinet member, and then I was removed from that government. And then I was, temporarily, sector commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say "the regime," you were critical of the regime, which regime were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the regime of Slobodan Milosevic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. Do you know whether or not General Strugar retired with an honourable discharge?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What about captain of the battleship, Milan Zec? Did he stay in the military and did he achieve any further positions after the Dubrovnik campaign?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was battleship captain, and he reached the rank of three star admiral, and then he retired quite normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral of the naval -- forces -- the naval forces of the JA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know when he retired?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He retired I think in 2000 or 2001, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, in May of 1992 was a group of high-ranking officers, generals included, retired by the regime? Was there a number of -- were a number of persons retired out by the regime?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. You had testified that officers of the 9th VPS and a cameraman had been sent to assess the damage caused to the Old Town as a result of the shelling of the 6th of December, and you sent them, I believe, on the 8th of December. You indicated that there had been video footage that they had taken. Had you seen that footage?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask, if we may, please, show a video, which by way of introduction is a video taken by the Croatians who are escorting the JNA officers who appear in plain clothes. And I will ask Admiral Jokic if he can assist us with identification of those officers. I also indicate to the Chamber that it is evident that this video was taped over Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. another video. There are, I think, two instances where you see -- it may have been stopped and then a commercial sector of what looks like a movie appears, a black and white. It appears to simply have been a re-tapeover [sic], so by way of explanation. Thank you. I think there's sound as well. Thank you

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There should be some sound, if we can stop for a moment, please. Yeah, it's background -- it may not be of much assistance, but there is some background sound that is ... If we're unable to proceed with sound, I ask that we go on and move ahead. I think it speaks for ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The date shown is 12th -- 8th of December, 1991. Stop please. Stop please. Could you go back for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, I'm going to ask you if you can identify --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Stop please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: These persons -- sorry. If you know or can identify these persons who are in raincoats or trenchcoats.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the middle is Captain Boskovic, my officer from the sector command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is this -- when you say "in the middle," is this the gentleman in the dark trenchcoat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I can ask my colleague, Ms. McCreath, to go back and get another still of the other gentleman, please, and to stop it as soon as he appears on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Stop. Stop please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recognise another person in civilian garb in this picture? Is it clear enough for you to see? Perhaps cut it to the side -- I'm sorry, it's not a very --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Pesic. I think it's Lieutenant Pesic. He's a lawyer. He spent very little time in the command. We took him in, I don't know how much before all of this happened. But it's him, yes, he was dealing with legal matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we move along as we get a better still, I will ask my colleague to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Something is not in the transcript. The transcript does not reflect that he was lawyer in the command of the sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's him. This is the Pesic, the man Pesic, the one in front. I mean, it's clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. And you had seen him before -- you had seen him at the time, in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like for -- to ask for a brief pause, please. The person that the person indicated now is quite different from the previous person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we've identified that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said that the previous person was also Pesic. So can he state his views accurately? Can he be shown both persons and say which one is Pesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think he has indicated clearly enough that this person in the light trenchcoat is, in his view, Pesic. He accepts that earlier he was mistaken when he identified another man. We would have to evaluate that in due course. Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, is that -- do you know, is that a cameraman who was also part of the contingent, if you know the face. Or if you don't, do you know a cameraman was, in fact, sent?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be certain. I don't know who the cameraman was. My memory fails me as far as that's concerned. I just know about the officers. A cameraman was engaged, but now who it was -- it was a civilian person. That's why I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, can I ask you, first of all, there were several individuals in white-type outfits, white-style outfits. Do you know from which organisation those persons have come that have joined the group of JNA officers, in the white outfits?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were the representatives of UNESCO or observers from the European Monitoring Mission. I know that some had white outfits, and others wore normal civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. Was the video footage which you viewed recorded by the officers from the JNA or from the 9th VPS similar in content to what you have just watched?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to substance, it is similar. But I cannot actually claim that I now identified all the details that I saw at the time. I seem to feel that this is far more impressive now. They have a greater impact, the images of the destruction and everything else now, looking at this footage now. But I would like to make two remarks in that regard, having said that. As far as I remember, on the footage I saw - or perhaps I got this mixed up - but above Onofrio's fountain, on the wall there was something written above that, and I think I saw that shown during the Milosevic trial. There was footage of what it said above the fountain. It said "What Onofrije built, Sofronije destroyed." Now I didn't recognise that or see it on this particular footage, and I remember the actual hit to the bell tower itself, the bell tower of the monastery in actual fact. At the top, there was a hole caused by a shell. I'm not sure if I missed it on this footage, but I don't recall having seen that. So those are my only two comments with respect to what I have just seen. All the rest I do believe corresponds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interpretation purposes. The witness said the bell tower of the monastery. It's not recorded in the transcript and it's important that it be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Admiral Jokic, was this the only contingent of JNA officers or representatives to tour the Old Town and record the damage -- now this damage is two days after the shelling, this is 8th of December. Do you know of any other group or contingent that was sent by you or by any in the 2nd Operational Group command or anyone else on behalf of the JNA to record the damage?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was the only group with that purpose in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you commented a few moments ago that this particular video was more impressive, what did you mean or what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that my impression, having seen this now, if I compare it to my impressions while I looked at it at the command in Kumbor, at the headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the translation of that last part. It was not -- I got it. Thank you. Do you know if you were shown or if the video which you saw had less damage shown, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult for me to say that now and to remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The damage which you have just seen on this video, in your view is it substantial or minor?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are substantial damages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At this time, this concludes the examination-in-chief. And I would like to tender into evidence, please, this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be marked as P145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jokic. Admiral, I am lawyer Goran Rodic, and I am Defence counsel for Pavle Strugar. I'm going to ask you some questions with respect to the answers you gave during the examination-in-chief, answers you gave to my learned friend of the Prosecution. My first question to you is this: Did General Strugar ever order you to attack or hit Dubrovnik and the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he issued these orders to anybody else to target Dubrovnik and the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, during the examination-in-chief you even said that in his orders there was express prohibition on opening fire on Dubrovnik and the Old Town. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me please, from what year to what year did you spend doing active service in the Yugoslav People's Army, between what period?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the naval academy in 1954, and I was retired -- I retired in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That makes it 38 years, I believe, of working service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You don't count the academy. From 1957. I misspoke. I joined the JNA in 1957, in actual fact, and worked there until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, in view of the duties and posts you held in the navy, did you have extra years of service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So with this extra years of service, did you have more than 40 years of service in actual fact? Did you surpass the necessary number of years?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but I wasn't old enough so I could stay on in the army for another four or five days [as interpreted], in view of the rank I had, just as other officers did and generals did, General Strugar being a case in point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Was it four or five days or four or five years, as we think we may have seen. The transcript says "days," "four or five days."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the course of your years of service in the army, were you promoted ahead of time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How many times did you receive fast promotion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, two years prior to the regular date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you ever punished in any way during your years of service, reprimanded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you always given good marks by your officers during your years of service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I always had very good and excellent marks accorded me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was your brother an active duty officer as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what he was.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He retired at his own request as a three star admiral in 1991, at the end -- or rather, during 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That means that you served the army at the same time, is that right, in the navy in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in part that would be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I assume that he held high military functions during his military career as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you enumerate some of them and tell us what the post was from which he retired.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief of staff in the fleet, then for many years he was head of the centre of military schools in Split and then served a time in Belgrade, where he was head of the high military schools. And his last post was assistant federal secretary for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say assistant to the federal secretary for logistics, or the rear, was he assistant to General Kadijevic, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How long during his actual term of office was he there occupying that post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for about a year and a half, almost two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I should just like to ask you to make a break between question and answer, because we're speaking the same language and they'll probably tell us to slow down and pause between question and answer. Is it true and correct that you were commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector between 1983 and 1988?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After that, what was your next post and position, your job?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1988, I was sent for extra training and education for one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What happened after that period of training?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that period of training, I went back to take up my duties as sector commander. And then subsequently I was sent to the government of Serbia, where I became secretary for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So that roughly corresponds, that post actually in a government corresponds to defence minister. Would that be it, although that's not what it was called at the time, but it would correspond to the function and post of Minister of Defence. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the first government of Prime Minister Stanko Radmilovic, that post was called Secretary of Defence. And then later on it became Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that you were sent from the post of commander of the military naval sector to the government of Serbia take up your duties there. Can you tell us a little bit more about how that came about, who sent you and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed to explain how this came about, with the Court's indulgence? In 1988, I was already proposed and nominated for the Secretary of Defence, I don't know who put me forward, but I went to the command of the then-military naval district Admiral Grubisic and told him I didn't want to take up that duty, that post, because I wasn't not well versed in that kind of business. I was a naval officer, that's the training I received, and I was educated as a naval officer, to perform that duty, so I said I didn't want to take up this new post.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you give me the name of the person who put you forward and how it came about from commander you went to take up the post of minister in the republican government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to state once again that I do not know who put my name forward for that post. And apart from that, I didn't complete what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I rejected this offer, another officer was put in that post. His name was Colonel Slobodan Mikic, he was appointed. And that was in 1988. And when I went to Kupari on one occasion for my holidays, I think Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that was in 1989, in the summer of 1989, when as part of my normal duties I received the federal secretary and I welcomed him at the airport, he said to me: "This time you won't be able to escape the post. And it would seem that we have to send you to Belgrade to take up your post."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, but could you tell us who the federal secretary was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kadijevic. I tried on that occasion, once again, to say that I don't think this would be a happy solution for me to take up that post. I tried to evade the issue. However, he said to me that this time that's how it had to be and that the officer, Mikic, that they had major problems with Officer Mikic and that he had to be replaced. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did you obey the federal secretary at the time, the federal secretary of national defence, General Kadijevic? Did you act accordingly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was nothing I could do. I listened to orders. I was sent to that structure and institution as an officer. I was dispatched there, as was the case in all other Yugoslav republics of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the federal secretary, Kadijevic, was he the man who put your name forward to occupy the post of minister?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know who did put you forward, if it was someone else?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I don't know. Quite possibly it might have been another general. I can't remember his name just now, but I'll remember it in due course, I'm sure. Anyway, he knew me and he would come to the coast for training exercises. At the time, he was the federal minister for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know Dusan Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would Dusan Mihajlovic at that time be the man who occupied a post in the government of the Republic of Serbia perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I understood your question to mean general, which general proposed me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm sorry to interrupt, but it's unclear about an answer that was just given to Mr. Rodic's question. The question was page 21, line 15: "Well, do you know who put you forward, was it someone else?" And the answer then goes on, and the last line says: "At the time, he was the federal minister for internal affairs." Is that a correct translation? Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed to explain. I have fully understood the question now, what is being asked of me --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Jokic. Not to waste time, because we're going to need a lot of time. Would you please answer my questions. Now, if I do something incorrectly, then Their Honours are there to caution me. So please do your best to answer my questions as succinctly as possible. I see that you are looking at the screen to see whether what I have said has been interpreted in the transcript, but that takes up quite a lot of time. It will be sufficient just make short breaks between my questions and your answers. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Specifically let me ask you this: Was it perhaps Dusan Mihajlovic, who at the time was a member of the Serbian government, who proposed you for Minister of Defence in the government of Serbia, that you should occupy that post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he wasn't in the government of Serbia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was he at that time, Dusan Mihajlovic, if he wasn't a member of the government?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, as far as I understood him, he was given the mandate of composing the Serbian government. However, when the government was actually formed, he became the first deputy prime minister. He didn't become the prime minister of that government.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who gave him the mandate to form a government for Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person in charge of that. I assume the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, who was the president of the republic at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a break then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, when Dusan Mihajlovic put your name forward for minister in the Serbian government, you said that at that moment he was not a member of government himself, if I understood you correctly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How much later after you had become minister did he, too, become member of the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was vice-president of the government. He was in charge of political issues. There were four vice-presidents. He, I assume, was the deputy in charge of political issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what Dusan Mihajlovic did just after he became a member of government. What did he do?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had been president of Valjevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You two knew each other well from Valjevo, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I hail from Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You are friends, aren't you? How long have you been friends?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were at the time. We had met each other and we were friends, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When did you meet?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were introduced by the then-president of the executive council of Valjevo municipality, Slobodan Djukic. We had grown up together, and he was the person who introduced me to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How long was that before Mihajlovic put your name forward for Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was a year earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time he put your name forward for that position, Mihajlovic was not involved in any private business?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. He had founded a party at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was the name of his party?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The New Democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me specifically the period of time that you spent as defence minister in the government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From November or December 1989 to the 31st of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As this was not a full term of office with the government, how did it come about that you left the position?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left that position because a conclusion had been reached that I was not supporting the government's policy. This was founded on several examples. They were not happy with my work as defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was this opposition between the government on the other hand and you as minister on the other reflected in?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, there were several times when I voted against the government's decisions. As far as I remember, the first time was about Slovenia and about the prices about of merchandise rising. I spoke out about this as a session of the government and I voted against it. Furthermore, I was asked to give my position on the Kosovo situation after I had been there. This was a coordination meeting, as they called it, which was also attended by President Milosevic. I put forward my position. I said that repression at Kosovo was counterproductive and that the policy should be changed -- or rather, that the rallies that were very -- that were massive at the time would become a rebellion. After I said that, I was never called again to offer my opinions at these coordination meetings. Also, when they were drafting the law on the national defence of Serbia, I proposed several solutions that were based on the federal law, meaning that the president of the republic had no authority to appoint the commander of Serbia's Territorial Defence, to promote him, or to remove him, or to command the Territorial Defence forces himself. I was in open opposition to that, so I was called by President Milosevic in connection with two articles that were related to that particular problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. As for your opposition in the government, your friend Mihajlovic, did he also vote against those decisions, or did he vote differently? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything about that, but I know that he criticised the government and he was in negotiations with the opposition parties at the time. And that's why he was removed from the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At the same time as you were or later?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a little before I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Briefly, while you were minister, did you work on any substantial projects or laws as a member of the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My most substantial task was to have this law on national defence passed as well as a plan of Serbia's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So were these passed during your term of office?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, neither were applied eventually, neither of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you did from the 31st of July, 1991, to the 7th of October, 1991, when you arrived in Kumbor to take up your duty as commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had been thrown out of the government on the 31st of July, and I was not assigned another duty. I was replaced by General Simovic. I left for the countryside, where I did some farming in my garden, my father's land.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you thrown out of the government or were you simply not re-elected? What was it really?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a reconstruction of the government, and three ministers were left out, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, the Minister of Defence, and I believe the minister who was in charge of liaising with Serbs outside Serbia, however I'm not sure about this latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was your role in 1990 and 1991 in relation to the areas in Croatia that were populated by Serbs in terms of arming?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no role in that. I was not involved. Specifically, there were requests by certain representatives who came to the government asking for assistance in terms of money, weapons, manpower, and so on. On several occasions I spoke to Prime Minister Zelenovic in order to arrange to give those people the assistance they requested. I remember two specific examples in connection with that. At that time, the Ministry of the Interior had taken over this work. I was not involved myself. My task --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were weapons being sent to Croatia at the time? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was minister, I didn't send any. I collected weapons that belonged to the Ministry of Defence, and then an order came for those weapons, communications equipment, to be handed over to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say that you had collected weapons in your capacity as defence minister, can you please elaborate on that. Where did you get the weapons from? What sort of weapons were those and where did you have it collected?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia's Ministry of Defence didn't have an army or weapons to give to the army. In our storages there were weapons that were no longer in use, infantry weapons, Soviet- and American-produced. There was a product, an idea, to sell these weapons, since the weapons were out of date. And there was an offer, or rather, a request by a man named Vasiljkovic who was willing to buy those weapons. However, this never materialised, because this was a form of assistance and these were not to be sold.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you sent those weapons as assistance to the Krajina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else do so?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on after I had gone, those weapons were handled through the Ministry of the Interior. I'm not sure through what channels exactly, but I heard later from General Simovic and others that the weapons had been sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Kumbor on the 7th of October to take up your new duty in the military naval sector, how did you get there and who travelled with you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After reporting, I took a plane from Belgrade with General Kadijevic and the president of Montenegro, Momir Bulatovic was also with him. We travelled as far as the Golubovci airport in Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During your flight with General Kadijevic, did you discuss your new position and the tasks awaiting you in the 9th Military Naval Sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss that. Back in Belgrade I was told by the chief of staff of the General Staff, General Adzic, that I would take up my duty as sector commander to replace Captain Djurovic, who had been killed. I expected that I would be briefed in greater detail as soon as I arrived in Podgorica, or rather, in Kumbor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You had spent three months without an assignment, and you were at home. And you, of all people, were selected. Do you think that the fact that you had been commander of the military naval sector for many years before that and the fact that you knew people in that military formation, that you enjoyed a position of authority among them, do you think that affected your appointment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think those reasons did affect my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you retired in May 1992, did you continue to live in Valjevo?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Until the end of 1992, I stayed in Herceg-Novi, but I suffered attacks there, personal attacks. So I had to sell my flat and go to Belgrade. I spent some time in Belgrade and some time in the countryside, near Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why did you come under attack in Herceg-Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The immediate reason was for me to leave immediately. I was assaulted once; there was an attempt. The way I ran the war, why I was so lenient with the Croats, why I allowed the Croats to get as far as Prevlaka. They said I was a traitor and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it one of your subordinate officers who told you this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was a group of civilians from the village of Zvinje near Prevlaka. They believed that I was to blame because of the lenient way in which combat was conducted and the way I treated the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Village of Zvinje, is it the same village that in late September 1991 on the border of Montenegro was shelled by the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This occurred before the Dubrovnik operation had begun, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Following your retirement, did you become a member of the New Democracy, Dusan Mihajlovic's party?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This party, was it part of Slobodan Milosevic's government until the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How long was it for then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I joined that party, it was not part of Serbia's government; it was in opposition. In 1993, I believe, when Dusan Mihajlovic became part of the government, I opposed that and I broke up relations with him for a year or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Wasn't Dusan Mihajlovic in that government from 1993 to 1997?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1996, something like that, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, was it perhaps until the autumn of 1997 in the government of Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in 1996 I was invited by the New Democracy to make our peace, and that I should work on the partnership for peace programme. In 1997, after the election results were rigged in Serbia - this was an election that had been lost by Slobodan Milosevic - I took part in the demonstrations for three months every single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right, Admiral. I asked you another question and I wanted an answer to that question. Let's not go beyond that. Can you tell me what position you held in the New Democracy party. Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was president of the committee for defence and counsellor for military affairs to the president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after you were retired when you became a member of the New Democracy, was that when Dusan Mihajlovic got into private business?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes, but I have nothing to do with that. I lived on my retirement pension. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, in the year 2000, after Milosevic was removed, did Dusan Mihajlovic become Minister of the Interior in the new Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, from October 2000 until October 2001 when the Prosecutor's indictment against you was unsealed, what did you do in the party or for Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't do anything. I was totally passive at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Again, General Aco Vasiljevic, was he in Dusan Mihajlovic's party? Did he hold a particular position in that party?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I worked on that partnership for peace programme, there were a few generals in the New Democracy party who assisted in this effort, among them General Aco Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the time when these things took place in 2001, General Vasiljevic was head of the security administration of the JNA -- in 1991, I stand corrected?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that after that, after a short break, he again held high positions within the security service in the Army of Yugoslavia later on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. In 1991 he was arrested, tried, and he spent about a year in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When was he activated again?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1999, until the aggression against Yugoslavia, until the bombing, he was passive. That's when I met him. I did not know him before that. When we worked on the project related to Yugoslavia's joining the partnership for peace. I worked with him then for about a year perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In October, November, and December 1991, was General Vasiljevic head of the security administration in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are the two of you friends?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained this to you. At that time, I did not know him. I met him in 1996, when I worked on the partnership for peace programme. He lived near my brother, and that's when we met and started socialising.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Dusan Mihajlovic, Minister of the Interior, brought you to The Hague himself -- or rather, that he accompanied you to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was he Minister of the Interior in February 2002, if I'm not mistaken, when you were provisionally released?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After you returned from The Hague, did he give you an official car and a security detail?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. This was upon the request of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did The Hague Tribunal ask that you be assigned an official vehicle and a personal security detail?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation I was given when I came to report, he explained to me that this was in line with the agreement on keeping me under control and protected while I'm provisionally released, and that this was at the request of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically whether in the written decision allowing your provisional release, did you see anywhere in that document that the MUP of Serbia was supposed to assign an official vehicle to you and a personal security detail? Or are some other conditions set forth there regarding your provisional release?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of these details; I don't know what you're referring to. I just know what the core of the matter is, that I had to be given protection, that I had to be under control, that there had to be reporting I think every month, in view of my movements. And those were the requirements of The Hague Tribunal. I'm not aware of the details involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were members of the MUP assigned to your personal security detail?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were always two men with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the period from when you were provisionally released until you returned to The Hague -- or rather, the 27th of August, when you entered your guilty plea, did you prepare your defence during that period?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of preparing your defence, did you talk to several witnesses who could have given you information that was useful for you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes. With the investigators -- together with the investigators, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you come to see these witnesses with a police escort in an official vehicle of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could not go by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was Dusan Mihajlovic Minister of the Interior in the government of the Republic of Serbia when you entered your guilty plea before The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Vladimir Kovacevic, nicknamed Rambo, indicted before this Tribunal, stated in the courtroom that through Minister Mihajlovic you organised a break into his apartment and that then his documents and cards were taken out of his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Quoting from another Chamber of the Tribunal, that is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not necessarily. I don't have to quote a different Trial Chamber -- proceedings before a different Trial Chamber. I can quote the media. This was published in newspapers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Simply put the question, Mr. Rodic, whether the witness knows of a break-in and whether he had any part in it, if that's what you're wanting to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jokic, do you have any knowledge about this, about the organisation of this break-in into Kovacevic's apartment, when his documents were taken away as well as military maps? Was that done in the organisation of the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I explain this? May I give a broader explanation in this regard, or should I briefly answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Answer the question I put to you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge that is even close to what you are talking about, and there is not a shred of truth in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you contact Kovacevic when you were provisionally released?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I contacted him before I came to The Hague, and if you wish I can tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: There is no need for you to do that. So these assertions made by Kovacevic are not true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not a grain of truth in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said that Vladimir Kovacevic, when you met him once, said that General Strugar gave him an apartment in Podgorica and that in return he gave him a passenger car. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's not only that he told me about this; several officers did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you work operationally in the field? Did you gather information for this kind of statement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked on my defence. This is what I was told by officers who were still active officers at the time and who knew the nature of this relationship and the details that I had no idea about whatsoever at the time of my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that you are not speculating with these data to the detriment of General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You claim that's the truth, what you said just now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that this is what I was told, what Captain Kovacevic said to me, at least two or three other officers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did people talk about you and was it even written in the newspapers, that you took war booty from the Dubrovnik theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can explain that, and there is evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please, I just put a brief question to you. Is that what was written and is that what people talked about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The witness did not complete what he wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He has answered the question. He wants to give a full explanation I suspect. It's something you could raise in re-examination, if Mr. Rodic doesn't pursue it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since you answer in the affirmative, was it that several persons said such things about you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The example is not the same. There was ambiguous writing about me in the newspapers, and what I claimed had to do with specific statements made by persons who knew about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. This person who wrote about you in the newspapers, do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vecernje Novosti which was the first newspaper to write about this, it was signed as: "A group of journalists from Vecernje Novosti". When I wanted to sue them, then they kept giving me these explanations. Who are you going to sue?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You could have sued the editor-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The editor-in-chief was linked to a man who led to the fact that I was attacked by given him presents, not only in Vecernje Novosti, but also newspapers in Montenegro, and television in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I have no intention of pursuing this in depth, but my question was whether, bearing in mind what you said just now, it must have been several persons who talked about this.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a question of persons. It has to do with a problem. If the Honourable Trial Chamber wishes, I can explain how come this campaign came to be, that I was proclaimed to be a robber and that the newspapers wrote about that and that Montenegro, General Strugar, and all other protagonists who took part in the looting decided to blame me. I can document this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to distribute some documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you read out what it says -- or rather, read through this certificate.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does this certify that the housing institution of 1313 military post Belgrade issues this certificate, according to its records, which show that Novica Vladimir Kovacevic, a retired army pensioner from Belgrade did not receive an apartment on any grounds from the military housing fund in the barracks of Podgorica. And that this certificate is being issued for purposes of the proceedings before the International Tribunal at The Hague and that the certificate was issued by the department for housing affairs in Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be allowed to explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please just answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is only part of the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: First of all, would you please say whether that is what the certificate suggests.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And if you would then tell me what you believe is the explanation for this certificate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the explanation is as follows: Captain Kovacevic was -- received an apartment but did not receive a document certifying to this allocation of an apartment and he told General Strugar: Unless I get it down in paper, I'm going to take the car back. When he didn't receive it on paper, because he wasn't able to get a document legally, then he took the car back and that was a new Peugeot car, and that's the real truth of it. After that their relations deteriorated and Captain Kovacevic was reassigned to Belgrade from Podgorica and that's the truth, the real truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And Captain Kovacevic told you all that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only him but two or three other officers have said so and I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Captain Kovacevic also said with respect to the people who stormed his flat -- apartment. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's not a grain of truth in that either, and if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I don't like anything. Just answer my questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've answered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document as a Defence exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be marked D40.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to another area. Is it true that the armed forces of the SFRY make up an entity and are composed of the Yugoslav People's Army and Territorial Defence? Of course I'm talking about the 1991 period, the material time.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that for the organisation and preparation of the armed forces, within the framework of their duties and competencies, pursuant to the constitutional law, it was the socio-political organisations that were responsible for that in basic organisations of associated labour and others, and the local community at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the competent authorities in the federation determined the basis and grounds for the organisation of the armed forces, the system of command and control, and all the bases for development plans and deployment plans for the use of the armed forces and also secure the unity of their action, and in keeping with that, organise and prepare the JNA as such?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in keeping with the fundamental premises for devising plans that the federal secretary of national defence passes regulations as to the manner and way in which plans are elaborated, development plans and deployment plans relating to the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the presidency of the SFRY as the highest organ of control and command over the armed forces is the supreme organ of control and command of the armed forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As a component of the armed forces of the SFRY, the Yugoslav People's Army is composed of the commands of the units and institutions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the General Staff represents just one of the command structures or, to be more precise, just one level of command in a united chain of command within the JNA as a component part of the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the General Staff is the staff of the supreme command. That is what it is in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When we talk about the organisational aspects, the JNA is made out of the ground forces, the navy, the airforce, and anti-air defence forces. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, how the full complement of the SFRY armed forces was reached.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually through mobilisation, if we're talking about the JNA. However, with the armed forces there was another way as well, volunteers would sign up to become members of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So this was through the reservists and the volunteers. That would be the method. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that the volunteers, from the moment they are accepted into the organisation by the unit commands to which they are attached, represent a component part of the armed forces themselves. They are part and parcel of the armed forces, and as such are subordinated to the united command of the armed forces themselves?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to the federal law on defence, that would be the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And when we're talking about the deployment and use of the armed forces, that is to say the JNA and the Territorial Defence of the then-SFRY, only the supreme commander - which meant the Yugoslav state presidency - had the power to decide on the deployment and utilisation of the armed forces and not the republican leaderships at all or the presidents of the republics. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what the law stipulates.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the republican leaderships in Croatia and Slovenia during that period of time prohibited their citizens from responding to the call-up from the JNA, and that those who were in its ranks already as soldiers or officers were told to leave the JNA without further ado?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During 1991, that is -- and I'm talking about 1991, a significant portion of the command cadre of the JNA, were they Slovene and Croat -- of Slovene and Croat ethnicity at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, paramilitary groups, did they represent armed formations of individual political parties, that is to say party armies but that they were never part of the armed forces of the SFRY. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it should have been by law; however, practice proved otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about 1991, at the time of the united SFRY, with its constitution, its laws, its military rules and regulations and all the rest of it, with the JNA and the Territorial Defence as the sole legitimate components of the armed forces of the SFRY, then the Croatian National Guard's corps would represent a paramilitary formation, a party army of the HDZ, which was the leading party on the Croatian political arena at the time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At the time, you were the Minister of Defence. And I assume that you were aware of the fact that the Yugoslav state presidency, as the supreme commander of the armed forces of the SFRY in wartime and in peacetime, already on the 9th of January, 1991, issued a decree on the disarmament of paramilitary formations with the deadline being the following ten days. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, did the JNA show a film to the Yugoslav public about the arming of Croatia, illegal arming of course, of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the film was organised by General Vasiljevic and it showed the arming of Croatia, Croatian formations being armed, led by Spegelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that individual members of the Yugoslav state presidency, the supreme command in fact, that is to say, individual presidency members, opposed the disarming and abolition of paramilitary formation, and they called them legal [Realtime transcript read in error "illegal"] armed forces of the republics within the composition of the SFRY. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
