utterances.text: I'm sure you'll remember similarly that after this order by the Yugoslav state presidency, the Croatian representatives, that is to say, Mr. Mesic and Mr. Tudjman, called for an additional two days for this disarmament process and that afterwards, after holding consultations with their allies from the Western countries, they refused this, to abide by this order on disarmament for the paramilitaries. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do believe that that's how it was, that that's what happened. They actually restructured these units and made them units of the legal SUP. I think they did something along those lines, and that's how they came to accept that presidency decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, can I just interrupt. An issue on the transcript confuses me. 44, line 12 it's put there, "illegal formations." At least in the English translation your question was "legal formations," not "illegal." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Legal formations, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. It just completely reverses the meaning in the transcript at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after this order issued by the presidency, the federal secretary for national defence and the staff of the supreme command four times put a proposal before the presidency to issue the order for disarmament, but that that never came about precisely because of the opposition by the secessionists, principally the Slovenian and Croatian secessionists within the presidency itself, of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that pursuant to a decision by the leadership of Croatia in the month of August 1991, a blockade was effected of all the garrisons and institutions of the JNA on the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Of course those attacks on the facilities and members of the JNA had taken place even before August. Do you know about that, in view of the fact that you were a naval officer, I'm sure you'll remember what happened in May 1991, for instance, in front of the headquarters of the naval military district in Split?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know what happened. It was the famous case of a soldier being strangled in an armoured tank in front of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is it true that on that occasion that soldier was killed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know how many soldiers and officers of the JNA in the course of 1991 were killed and massacred in different towns throughout Croatia in the barracks and outside the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you an exact figure, but I know that the number was considerable. There were quite a number of soldiers and officers that suffered that fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there any attacks being carried out by the paramilitary units of the Republic of Croatia against military convoys? Was there any looting of JNA property?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Federal Government, as early as June 1991, started proceedings before the institutional -- constitutional court to stop the establishment of the National Guard's Corps as a military formation and to characterise it as an illegal and unconstitutional act?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 16th of October, 1991, the constitutional court passed a decision on the illegality and nonconstitutionality of the establishment of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably. I can't remember any details, but I'm sure this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I assume you were in touch and were familiar with the situation in the garrisons of the military naval district in the period of 1991 under consideration. Can you tell us more about this. Were there any attacks being carried out against soldiers, military officers, their families perhaps, any military facilities? Were there any blockades of barracks within the military naval district?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the barracks for the most part. The Ploce garrison had been attacked I believe in August 1991 and losses were inflicted on the soldiers who were standing guard near the warehouse in which weapons were being kept. There were attacks in Sibenik as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about Zadar, Pula?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zadar too. As for Pula, I think the situation was more peaceful there, in Pula, and in Rijeka. The most difficult situation was in Zadar and Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Split is where the headquarters of the military naval district were. What was the situation like over there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were several attacks in Split on the two barracks. Weapons were being seized. There was a convoy of APCs that was attacked once, and a company of APCs was seized and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the command of the military naval district, did it have to move from Split?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because conditions became unbearable. It was impossible to exercise command. The command of the military naval district was evacuated to the island of Vis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the other units belonging to the command of the military naval district? Did they remain on the blockade? What happened to Divulje, Lora, the military ports?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Divulje garrison was blocked at the time as well as the military port of Lora.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The JNA members who were under blockade, was their electricity cut off, their water supplies? Did they have problems getting food supplies into their barracks?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the first moves that were made, cutting off their water and electricity supply, making sure that no food reached them inside the barracks, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there any operations carried out by paramilitary units against the barracks and garrisons? I mean operations in terms of firing.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Attacks were carried out against the barracks in Split and other barracks, too. I remember the military command post of the military naval district, which was in a building near Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did anyone get hurt, any members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The JNA and the presidency of the SFRY, did they demand the removal of blockade against their facilities on several occasions? What happened in terms of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were daily contacts or very frequent contacts at any rate between the top leadership of the JNA and the presidency on the one hand and the Croatian authorities on the other. There were contacts with the leadership and with local authorities in some of the towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it not correct that several times during those negotiations, and even when agreements were signed, Republic of Croatia promised to remove the blockade of military garrisons and military facilities in Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were promises that were being made all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that those demands were never met and the agreements were never complied with, but rather that the attacks against the military facilities intensified, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know more about the military facilities along the Adriatic coast. As for the other facilities, I know from the press, from the media, while I was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The situation is more or less the same, but at least as far as you know about the Adriatic coast, about the military naval district, is it true that I said a while ago, what I stated, about those agreements being violated by the Republic of Croatia and that the attacks against those facilities continued or grew in intensity, if anything, in the military naval district?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, that's true. I'm only talking about some details that I can't confirm, but on the whole, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the units of the military naval district in 1991? Were they being transferred, or rather, evacuated from garrisons in Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on agreements that were reached concerning the evacuation of units from the Republic of Croatia, the evacuation commenced of all the garrisons between the Italian border in the north, I think that was the Pula sector, and as far as south as Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This evacuation of the units of the military naval district from the Republic of Croatia, when did it reach a peak in terms of intensity?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of intensity, it peaked between November and January, November 1991, January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we say the period between November 1991 and January 1992 then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In that period of time in the course of the evacuation, did attacks against members of the JNA, their property and families, continue?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Units of the military naval district, where were they evacuated to for the most part? Into which other area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those units were evacuated to Montenegro between the Boka Kotorska coast and as far as the port of Bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about a lot of military equipment, weapons, military resources, was it left behind in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They just couldn't evacuate everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did this later come into the possession of the paramilitary units, the National Guard Corps, the Croatian navy, and other military units within the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to something else now. Can you tell us, please, in the territory of the former SFRY at the time, there existed the 1st Military District with headquarters in Belgrade, the 3rd Military District with headquarters in Skopje, the 5th Military District with headquarters in Zagreb, military naval district. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that these formations of the JNA in terms of military districts throughout SFRY territory were not necessarily limited in terms of territory to the republican borders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the whole idea, that military districts should not coincide with republican borders in order to avoid identification of the army with a certain republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This means that each of the military districts covered a certain area or a certain territory or extended over the territories of at least two, some military districts even three republics, that made up the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, what you have in front of you is a map of the SFRY. Can I please ask you to use a felt pen or a marker. Just make sure it's not red or blue. Can I ask you to please mark on the map just next to Belgrade. Can you put the 1st Military District, the abbreviation there, the 1st VO, I think that was the reference at the time. Is that the abbreviation that stood for the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, may the marking be done while the map is on the ELMO so we can observe the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Skopje and Macedonia, we have the headquarters of the 3rd Military District, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In Zagreb we have the headquarters of the 5th Military District, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In Split, the headquarters of the military naval district. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This mark, VPO, can you just please draw an arrow to Split from there.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember, roughly speaking, the territorial borders under the jurisdiction of these military districts and the military naval district. Can you please first tell me if you remember the respective borders of each of these.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the military naval district, it extended from the Italian border as far as Kopar [phoen], covered part of Slovenia, Istria, the Rijeka general area, Zadar, Sibenik, Split, part of the Ploce area, Dubrovnik, the Montenegrin coast extending as far south as the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please use this blue felt pen and draw the borders of the military naval district. You can put it in front of you, if you find that more convenient.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we please have that placed on the ELMO for all to see. Tell me, please, do you think you could draw the borders for the other military districts in the same way, roughly speaking. I'm not asking for any great degree of precision. The 5th Military District, for example, did it cover Slovenia, Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 5th Military District covered the Republic of Slovenia, with the exception of the coastal area; Croatia, but not entirely; part of Bosnia and Herzegovina; the Bihac area; something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Military District --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Sarajevo was also included in the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the largest part of Serbia except for the area around Nis and Bosnia and Herzegovina, so this entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Within the Skopje area, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I don't know the exact details right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Military District included Macedonia, part of the Nis area, and part of Montenegro. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask that this map be assigned a number, please. I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This map is marked D41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a break, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, we have explained -- or rather, before the break, we explained the territorial distribution of the military districts of the Yugoslav People's Army, and I should now like to ask you to tell me the military naval district, how many men -- or rather, how many sectors did it have within the district and which they were, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military naval district had three military naval sectors, five in the military naval district of Pula -- or rather, there was Pula --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the 5th Military District or Sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I misspoke, I meant the sector, and the headquarters of that 5th Military Naval Sector was in Pula, the 8th with its headquarters in Sibenik, the 9th Military Naval Sector in Kumbor, in the Bay of Kotor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So the entire military naval district had three military naval sectors, regardless of the numbers in the heading of each sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There were three sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And can you explain the competencies and authority -- or rather, the territory that was covered by the 9th Military Naval Sector, for example, in Boka, the bay of Kotor, or rather in Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th Military Naval Sector of Boka covered the territory from Neum, and then in the hinterland from 5 to 20 kilometres in depth to the border with Albania. The broader region around Ulcinj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher for her assistance now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, would you do what you did a moment ago with the other map and mark on this map the territory covered by the 9th Military Naval Sector. Would you draw the line around the territory covered by that sector, the 9th Military Naval Sector.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Underneath, there's the Adriatic Sea, and could you put in the 9th VPS underneath that, please, military naval sector. Thank you. So the upper borders were the town of Neum. That was where, within the frameworks of the Bosnia and Herzegovina republican frontiers, you have the outlet to the sea. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the last reaches were in Montenegro, below Ulcine, bordering on Albania?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And the lake Skadar, because of the facilities on the lake also came under the authority of the 9th Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of these borders, these territorial borders that you have outlined for us, does that include Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should now like to have a number assigned to this document, to the Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Defence exhibit, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This map will be marked D42.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know at that time that in the SFRY there existed military courts which were in Ljubljana, Zagreb, Split, Sarajevo, Belgrade, Nis, and Skopje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The military court in Split, territorially speaking, did it come under the competence and authority of the entire territory covered by the entire military naval district?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: By the same token, that would mean that the military court in Split, territorially speaking, covered the area of the 9th Military Naval Sector. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, if you know about this, in view of the situation, during 1991 - and I think you've already explained to us what was happening to the command of the military naval district in Split - do you know what happened to the military court in Split?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is this: When I arrived to my command or headquarters towards the end of October/beginning of November, the military court from Split was evacuated to the Bay of Kotor. And I- at their request, at the request of the court itself- I provided them with accommodation in the JNA centre in Tivat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that only two judges from -- or the team of judges in the Split military court, which had its headquarters there, came to Tivat, were evacuated to Tivat with all the archives belonging to the military court?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were very few of them. I remember Stanivuk. I think he was the prosecutor, I believe, and that he communicated with me with respect to putting it up. There were very few people with them and they needed a month or two to set themselves up and create the necessary conditions for work, to have all the manpower they needed to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't have the requisite number of judges necessary to make up a trial chamber, for them to be able to function according to the letter of the law. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I understand the technique used is to make a statement and then ask: Is that right? But it's bordering very much on Defence counsel's testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be much more persuasive and helpful, Mr. Rodic, if you were to see whether the witness knew the answer rather than you telling him the answer and then asking if it was correct. Just a mild modification of the way you approach it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I will reword the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the military court, which was put up in Tivat, did not have a requisite number of judges for it to be able to function pursuant to the law governing military courts?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that communication with the prosecutor, Mr. Stanivuk, he told me that they were having problems and they couldn't function because they didn't have enough people to work with them. Now, I don't know what they lacked, whether they didn't have enough judges or prosecutors or other members of the staff, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But did you know at the time that the judges of the military court who were Croats by ethnicity, they stepped down from the military court, they left, and stayed on in Croatia and were not evacuated with the other staff? They didn't go to Tivat.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know they remained in Split. And my legal advisor who I had in the command also left. He was allowed by the command to leave and he went to Split. His name was Captain Barbaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In response to a question by my learned colleague in the examination-in-chief, when she asked you about an indictment raised in the military court in Sarajevo against a military recruit by the name of Veselin Simovic [phoen] for multiple killings of a number of civilians in a village near Trebinje, you said you were aware of that event, that you knew of it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That military recruit, was he within the framework of the composition commanded by General Eremija, the conscript in question?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to meet General Eremija on the occasion of the command post of the 2nd Group in Trebinje after that event?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What were your impressions of General Eremija at that time? Did he tell you what had happened at the command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was sick with worry over that case -- or rather, his ulcer was playing up as a result of it. And I don't know whether he went to hospital, whether he was hospitalised, but he was very ill. He looked sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did he say he had had a heated discussion with General Strugar about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that General Strugar cut him short, if I can use that rather military term.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say "cut him down" or "cut him short," would that mean that General Strugar was angry and told him off with respect to that case or something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In 1991, while you were the commander of the military naval sector of Boka on the 7th -- from the 7th of October, in October, November, and December 1991, in that period, was a state of war declared?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A state of war was not declared then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In view of the situation on the ground in the area and the tasks assigned to the unit, their life and work and the prevailing conditions during October, November, and December 1991, the fact that a state of war had not been declared, did that represent a great obstacle to command and control over the JNA units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was absolutely right. It was a considerable obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you explain that to Their Honours, please, at least this comparison that you had to work as if it was peacetime, whereas in fact the situation was quite the reverse and different and the commanders had quite different competencies and authorisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Counsel is testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are there, very clearly, giving a lecture, Mr. Rodic. You're not the witness; the witness is sitting over there. Could you let him do the speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I'll reformulate my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This difficult situation for purposes of control and command, because a state of war had not been declared, can you elaborate and tell us how these difficulties were reflected on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fact that the units were engaged in operations, that people were being killed and wounded, meant that we had a war situation in which the laws applied during wartime should have been applied at that time, too. However, the commanders engaged in combat activities and who commanded the units themselves frequently were not in a position to behave as they would otherwise and to bring to task anybody who was engaged in unlawful acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, these laws and regulations and rules that come into force once a state of war has been declared, are they much stricter than the laws, rules, and regulations that are implemented in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Those laws, rules, and regulations that come into force during a state of war, are they far more summary in character when it comes to sanctions for any negative conduct? Let me just add, do they have greater powers and authorities, that is to say the commanders. Do they wield greater power and authority in enforcing sanctions against any negative conduct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. And I remember one specific example, if I might be allowed to expound, Your Honours. When I asked my legal officer what I could do in order to punish individuals who violated regulations with respect to the use of weapons, he consulted the law books. And pursuant to that law in wartime, there are no discussions of this kind for disciplinary errors or transgressions, and I wasn't clear on that, what he meant by that or misdemeanors, whether because there was time to do so, whether that was why just more grievous acts were punished, those that came under the military courts to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You should like to ask you for the transcript - it doesn't seem to be clear looking at the transcript - what your legal officer actually told you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My legal clerk at the headquarters explained to me that during a state of war, small misdemeanors and offenses, which would otherwise be punishable during peacetime and the perpetrators punished, during wartime go unpunished because military courts have to focus on crimes, actual crimes, rather than offenses and misdemeanors.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, those laws, rules, and regulations which are effective during wartime are stricter and more effective, that is to say, are all the proceedings speeded up in wartime?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are stricter, and that's why they are very often referred to as court martials or something like that, which are established, if the need arises, in addition to regular military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The laws, rules, and regulations which are effective during a war situation, do they help commanders in being more effective in their functions of command and control?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When a state of war is declared, are war military courts established then, attached to headquarters of military districts, divisions, units, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that is how the law regulates that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So instead of one military court that works in peacetime, if a state of war is declared, four or five courts are established for a certain military formation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it is, according to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the period of October, November, and December 1991, such a situation did not exist -- or rather, there were no war military courts because a state of war had not been declared?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what is the role of the organs of military security and military police in the JNA in terms of crime prevention and control?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their task was in accordance with the law in peacetime and of course in war that whenever military men in various units broke the law in any way, they were supposed to investigate, to file criminal reports and to hand this over to an investigative judge in order to have the proceedings carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Security organs and the competent authorities of the military police, when engaged in crime prevention and control, were they independent in the JNA, in the exercise of these duties?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did have their independence, but within the command. The commands could have some influence in terms of their own requests regarding particular cases. But independently of the command, they were duty-bound by the rules of service to do their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The security organs of the military police, in peacetime are they attached to commands of units and institutions in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The security organs of the military police, from the point of view of military establishment, are they subordinated to the security administration of the JNA as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Along the vertical line, they are subordinated to the security administration, especially in this professional line of work of theirs, in the protection of the units that they are in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When we talk about the military police in the JNA, within the military police are there duty services with officers who are engaged in crime control?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a duty service, and I think that there is a crime technician or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is there a difference in terms of work in the control and prevention of crime between the officers who are in charge of that particular line of work and the crime technician on the one hand and ordinary military policeman on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There has to be a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that an ordinary military policeman cannot be engaged in that line of work, that he has other tasks within the activity of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An ordinary military policeman is not trained to carry out such work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When we previously discussed the situation in the SFRY in 1991, the situation in the JNA in that particular time and at that particular place, did this negative situation have any bearing on the work of military security and military police in view of all the difficulties that we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. It had to have a bearing, like on all commands and units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me in terms of members of the JNA and the armed forces as a whole, how were they affected by a situation in which some members of the supreme command were opposed to disarming paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this had to have a negative effect, certainly, on all members of the Yugoslav People's Army. Namely, that there was a certain lack of confidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does it have a negative affect on the military when some members of the supreme command desert?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What is the effect on the military when top military officers, for example, the commander of the air force, commits desertion and becomes chief of the General Staff of the opposite side, which was a paramilitary formation at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly has a negative effect. I'm sure that you bear in mind General Tus, that is who you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, he was a retired man. I think that he retired in the month of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that he immediately came to the head of the General Staff of the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you know Nojko Marinovic well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how this came about.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was commander of the sector, in the period from 1983 until 1988, Nojko Marinovic was a major and chief of staff of the 472nd Brigade. And I then cooperated with him because at that time the brigade was subordinated to the Boka sector. He was a highly professional officer, well-trained, strict and brilliant from every point of view. I had also put his name up for a speedy promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As for the military of the 472nd Brigade, did his abandoning that brigade in the situation when he had mobilised it have a negative affect?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, an absolutely negative affect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As for the military of the 472nd Brigade, was it adversely affected by the situation when he, although he had previously mobilised that unit and developed that unit and then aware of its positions, shelled the brigade from the other side and on the 1st of October kill eight soldiers from his former brigade?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, we're relying on facts not in evidence. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How can you justify that, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the foundation is in the testimony of some witnesses. I'll remind you of one witness at least who confirmed this, Nikola Samardzic who at that time was a minister in the government of Montenegro. He testified before this Honourable Trial Chamber. There are also documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think any of the evidence has gone into the detail that you're dealing with here. There is detail of Major Marinovic having joined the Croatian side, but you were putting in your question here very specific actions by him and their consequences, none of which I recall in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the killing of eight soldiers at Ivanjica, there certainly was a reference to that because I asked Witness Samardzic a question in relation to that. My only mistake may have been to phrase the question immediately in terms of Nojko Marinovic killing someone, which I apologise for. But I would be happy to rephrase my question along the lines of Nojko Marinovic as commander of the Croatian forces, which means that the forces under his command perpetrated those acts, which led to the killing of some soldiers from his former brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you see the problem and you see the solution. Go ahead, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, is it true that these soldiers from Trebinje Brigade, eight of them, the soldiers I referred to at the beginning, on the 1st of October were killed by the Croatian forces at that time that time under the command of Nojko Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were killed at Ivanjica by a mortar shell, a 120-millimetre mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please enumerate for me which units establishmentwise were part of the 9th Military Naval Sector, that's as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean establishmentwise, which units?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the naval components, it had the 16th Border Naval Detachment with patrol boats to secure the sea border; it also had a mixed division on ships for military landing used for transport and for landings; it also had a rocket battery, a sea/land rocket battery, the 69th Rocket Base; and anti-aircraft defence division; the 367th Military Naval Logistics base; there was a unit for reconnaissance observation and reporting, so-called 9th Company; and prior to my arrival there was also the 472nd Brigade within its composition until as late as the 25th of September, which is when it was resubordinated directly to the command of the 2nd Operational Group. And there was the 2nd Staff Unit. If necessary, I can enumerate them for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I don't think that's necessary. Thank you. The 472nd Brigade from Trebinje, establishmentwise, was it part of the 9th Military Naval Sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, it used to be in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the period of time between 1983 and 1988 or 1989, which is when you were also commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector, this brigade, 472, establishmentwise, even then was it part of the 9th Military Naval Sector or not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In terms of establishment, its composition did not change throughout 1991, with the exception of the period when the operation began, the one we're talking about. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It didn't change much, but there was a large turnover in terms of the command staff, in terms of the officers, and manpower. It was no longer the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you talk about changes to the composition of manpower and officers, what was this caused by?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was caused by a disturbance in relations, which led to an internal conflict within the Republic of Croatia. So that areas under the Croatian authorities refused to contribute to the mobilisation into the JNA units that had been trained in those areas --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, that had been set up in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Regardless of all these changes for example in the period between 1983, which is the first time when you were sector commander, and the 25th of September, was this brigade still under the control and command of the 9th Military Sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I said before, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In relation to these problems in connection with the manpower and officers of the 472nd Brigade, as well as other units, was this affected by the negative circumstances prevailing in the country, the sort of thing we've referred to, mobilisation problems and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there problems with maintaining manpower levels as far as the regular units were concerned in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the problems were huge. The biggest problems were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All together this affected the combat readiness and the level of training of that particular brigade, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly this would have had a very negative effect on combat readiness and combat morale and the way the unit was used in combat, and what the unit was capable of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Following this restructuring in September until as late as the 16th of October, 1991, the 4th Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade, was it directly resubordinated to the 9th Military Naval Sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On my arrival, I found the 4th Battalion there. On the 8th of October, it had been taken out of combat and it was on leave in Igalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the 4th Battalion of that brigade was only transferred from your jurisdiction on the 16th of October?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but they did not receive any kind of combat orders from me between the 8th and the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But that's not what my question was about, so if you could just please briefly answer my questions specifically. We'll get to that later, the combat orders. What about the other units under your command in the period between the 16th of October and the 25th of October, 1991? Did they have any contact or coordination with that battalion, the 4th Battalion, of the 472nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When the 4th Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade was transferred, moved, from your zone of responsibility on the 16th of October between the 8th of October -- between the 16th of October and the 25th of October, did the remaining units under your command have any point of contact or any cooperation with that specific battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. This battalion left for the left flank. It was still part of the brigade. And between my units and that battalion, you had Croatian units. That's until the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that after the 25th of October, the whole 472nd Brigade returned to their original unit, the 9th Military Naval Sector, and were again under your command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was only a temporary thing. This lasted a couple of days only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may just be allowed one final question in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The 472nd Motorised Brigade, between the 25th of October and the 21st of November, 1991, was it part of the 9th Military Naval Sector and as such directly subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Formally, yes, but I should need to explain this to Their Honours, this is no simple fact, the way you make it seem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, we're running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But my questions will be along the same lines, so you will get a chance to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It seems that if Your Honour would be good enough to allow the question, that a complete answer should be allowed without interruption from counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we're going to follow the matter up when we resume tomorrow. We will adjourn for the day now, and the evidence will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: at 1.46 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
